documentation:
## Large-Scale Turbulent Fire

### What it does

This graph illustrates how to set up a large-scale simulation of turbulent flames using Aero and how to render it with high detail using a shader network in Arnold.

### Inputs and outputs

The graph is self-contained except for the Arnold shader network which is referenced from the graph.

### How it works

- The emission is controlled by `setup_emission_fields` which creates a combination of two regions of randomized fog density and temperature fields that are input to the `source_air` node.

- The collisions are input via the `collider` node and is comprised of a single ground collider.

- `setup_influences` creates a set of influence fields that add small-scale noise, medium to large scale turbulence as well as wind to the simulation.

- The `aero_solver_settings` node defines the simulation settings, including a simulation bound that erases the higher parts of the smoke plume.

- The `simulate_aero` compound takes as input the emission, collision, influences as well as settings nodes and runs the simulation.

- The output from `simulate_aero` is fed through `post_process_temperature` before rendering to dampen temperatures that lead to red flames not present in reference footage, but which may be present in the simulation output.

- Finally, materials for rendering are assigned depending on the renderer via the `assign_material__arnold` and `assign_material__viewport` nodes respectively. The `assign_material__arnold` references an Arnold shader network which brings out additional high detail in the Arnold render. It is currently not possible to apply this to the viewport render.

_notes.text: This compound post processes the voxel_temperature property to dampen temperatures that lead to red colors when rendered with a blackbody shader. The red tones appear approximately below 1000 degrees Celsius and are often not present in reference footage, hence we apply this step to remove them. An f-curve determines where to dampen the temperatures. The exact cutoff temperature used in the f-curve depends also on the "Temperature" and "Blackbody Kelvin" multipliers used on the Arnold_standard_volume material definitions. In particular, if these multipliers are above 1, the f-curve cutoff must be less than 1000.

We assign a different material depending on whether we are rendering with Arnold or directly in the viewport.
The Arnold shader can be inspected in the Hypershade. It utilizes a small shading network that activates the temperature only in a small band near the edge of the flames. This captures the highly detailed look of real diffusion flames where a thin sheet of glowing soot surrounds a cooler darker interior.
The viewport shader does not yet support this shading network so it will give less detail. The set_viewport_volume_settings node disables the "Geometry Depth Test" option for faster viewport interaction.

# Aero Source

The source consists of a flat cylinder geometry inside which fog density and temperature are emitted by the use of scalar fields. The scalar fields add time-dependent noise to the fog and temperature. The emission area is comprised of a small dense emission area and a bigger less dense surrounding emission area. A radius and random seed can be used to control and vary these emission areas. The diagnostics on setup_emission_fields can be enabled to view the emission fields.

The default detail size used is 0.1 - a low resolution setup for faster iteration times, the high resolution of 0.025 will deliver highly detailed production-quality but also more time-consuming simulation. 

Even though the output of the simulation looks like flames due to rendering with a black body shader, the simulation itself is just an aero simulation without any combustion.

# Influences

The influences consist of a variety of different effects:
* A fractal_disturbance_influence adds small scale noise and breaks up smooth mushroom plumes.
* A vorticity_influence amplifies small scale rotation.
* A number of turbulence_influences add rotational structures at various scales, from medium to large.
* A wind_influence gives the overall direction of the wind.
* A dissipation_influence dissipates the fog in areas where the flames cool down and turn into smoke.

# Colliders

A ground plane is added as a collider to better capture the look of flames near the ground where air can only flow in from the sides.

# Solver Settings

The simulation_bounds ensure that the simulation grid does not grow indefinitely as the smoke moves upwards.

The "Style" is set to "busy" to retain the most detail. If artifacts appear, "Style" can be set to "fluffy" to better retain detail without artifacts, but at the cost of losing a bit of detail compared to "busy".

The "Min Steps" and "Max Steps" are both set to 4 to match the look of running the simulation at 120 FPS with  "Min Steps" and "Max Steps" set to 1. However, these can be reduced for faster simulation times, but will also cause the simulation to look slightly different. In general, fewer steps will lead to hotter flames and more crisp detail.

# density and temperature

Fog density and temperature are emitted by the use of scalar fields.
The scalar fields add time-dependent noise multiplied by global multipliers "fog_density_multiplier" and "temperature_ multiplier" to the fog density and temperature respectively.

The emission area is comprised of a small dense emission area and a bigger less dense surrounding emission area. A radius and random seed can be used to control and vary these emission areas.

# ground emission

The ground_emission constructs a flat cylinder geometry randomized in the radial direction to create a randomly jagged but largely circular emission geometry.
A radius and seed are used to control the 
size and randomness of the geometry.

# sphere field
A sphere_field is used to control falloff of the random noise used in the emission away from the center of the ground_emission geometry.

# voxel field
A voxel_field is used to limit emission to fall inside the ground_emission geometry volume.

# fractal noise
A time-dependent fractal_noise_field adds random noise to the emission.

# max
The max ensures that only positive noise values contribute to the emission.

# fractal noises
To create the desired density and distribution of random noise inside the emission gemetry, a number of time-dependent fractal_noise fields are combined. 

Please double-click the compound to see how
